zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Review aid (not transcribed): The supplied page subset of Entry Words Data of Nippojisho was consulted after an independent scan reading for lexical identification and coverage. NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510; CC BY 4.0. Source: https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html ; license: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ . The returned transcription choices and English line notes are this reviewer’s scan-based work, not a copied NINJAL transcription.

lines.note: Guioxǔ here is an honorific vessel, Vonfune, unlike the fishing-boat homophone closing f241. The joined spelling of Vonfune is visible and retained.

runs.text: vai algum ſenhor, ou peßoa honrada.

lines.note: The boat carries a lord or another honored person. This completes the reason for the respectful Japanese expression.
Guioxut, paraphrased Von ide, denotes a ruler’s or great lord’s departure. Se- begins senhor across the physical break.
Nhor grande completes the great-lord alternative. The short continuation closes the honorific departure entry.
Guioyǔ describes fish at play, particularly leaping. A clear caron marks the final u; the draft omitted this visible mark.
The example begins with the waves being quiet and the fish playing. Guio- is divided at the printed hyphen and completed below.
Yǔ completes guio-yǔ; the caron is visible, not a grave. Fodo baxiru is retained as printed rather than regularized from the expected Japanese expression for leaping or splashing.
The Portuguese completes the picture of fish leaping with the sea and waves quiet. This is the example’s continuation, not an independent gloss.
Guiǒzǒ denotes a figure or image; both Catachi tokens and both carons are preserved. The alternative Portuguese noun continues below.
Estatua supplies statue as the second gloss of Guiǒzǒ. Its short physical line is retained separately.
Guiǒzui is bathing, explained by Yuuo abiru. The Portuguese begins washing the body and specifies the water in the continuation.
The water is hot; Guiǒzui ſuru gives the verbal example. The headword’s repeated o is abraded, but the surviving curve and the entry above support the reading.
Guiqet, literally an ant’s hole, is a cavity or nest of ants. The final t represents the printed checked ending rather than an omitted modern syllable.

Guiraguirato is explicitly adverbial, describing the manner of shining or glittering. The enlarged stop after the Japanese word has a descending tail and is read as a comma; Adu. is the italic grammatical label.
Reſplandecer completes the alternative verb for shining. Its final stem vowel is e, not OCR o, and the clause refers back to the shining object.
Guirameqi gives the verb for gleaming, with ficari as a related Japanese expression. The printed principal-part abbreviations and comma sequence are not expanded.
The figurative extension is to show liveliness and zeal. Moſtrar and viueza correct lexical OCR confusions in Moftrar and vtueza; Pertranslat. remains unexpanded.
The zeal is displayed in service. Carega fôcôua begins an example about that person’s service, and fa- begins the twenty-day expression continued below.
Tçuca completes fa-tçuca, twenty days; the example describes a twenty-day burst of zeal. The Portuguese O ſer begins serviço without a visible terminal hyphen.

runs.text: uiço daquelle durara cõ feruor por vinte dias.

lines.note: Uiço completes ſer-uiço. The person’s service will remain fervent for twenty days; feruor corrects OCR feruer, while the unaccented durara is preserved.
Guireo, explained by doubting and considering, is uncertainty or doubt. The initial G is visible, not OCR C.
Guiri is sound reasoning or a good account, Yoqi cotouari. The visible arre- begins arrezoamento, rather than the draft’s arra-.
The example concerns whether the reasoning of this book can be followed. Cuda- is completed by the negative ranu below.

Ranu completes cudaranu; qicoyenu gives the alternative negative, not OCR qicoyeiu. The n is worn, but its remaining strokes and the following explanation support the negative form: the reasoning cannot be understood.

runs.text: mento deſte liuro não ſe entende. ¶ Item,

lines.note: Mento completes arrezoamento. The translation says that the book’s reasoning is not understood, then Item introduces another sense of Guiri.
The second sense is refinement or scrupulous propriety. Guirino fucai fito illustrates a person possessing this quality deeply.
De grande primor completes the characterization of that refined or scrupulous person. It does not refer back to the book’s argument.

Guirio denotes strength or good bodily condition, explained by Tçuyô ſucuyacana. The unaccented headword is retained: the faint matter above its final o does not securely establish a caron, although the next entry and the post-reading NINJAL checkpoint suggest Guiriǒ. Tçuyô retains the draft’s circumflex; only one arm prints strongly.
Ças completes for-ças, followed by good bodily disposition. This closes the physical-vigor definition.
Guiriǒna characterizes a person with strength and good constitution. The caron is clear; the Portuguese Peßoa has no secure tilde, so the draft’s õ has been removed.
Guiron combines contention and discussion, Araſoi, ronzuru, and is glossed Diſputa. The damaged initial is G rather than OCR C.
Guitai here is hesitation or stalling, explained by Cori todocouoru. The Portuguese begins stopping or lingering, whose circumstances follow below.

runs.text: rar, não ſe reſoluendo a fazer algũa couſa, ou

lines.note: Rar completes pa-rar. The hesitation consists in failing to resolve to do something; the printed negative and algũa are retained.

runs.text: não dando reposta de ſi, ou de não, &c.

lines.note: The alternative is not giving a yes-or-no answer. Reposta and si are the visible historical forms and are not modernized to resposta or sim.
A separate Guitai entry means doubt. Guitaini voyobu gives the construction for falling into doubt or becoming doubtful.
Duuidar translates the preceding example with a single infinitive. The entire short row remains body text.
Guiuacu combines doubt with bewilderment, Vtagai madô. Duuidas corrects the draft’s Duaidas; er- continues the second Portuguese noun.
Ros completes er-ros, errors. The following upright S. is a written-register label rather than part of the italic noun.
Guiǔba pairs cattle and horses, Vxi, vma. The Portuguese says Bois & caualos; the clear gap before & contains no comma.
Guiǔca is a cattle house or shed, literally Vxino iye. The final S. is upright and marks written usage.
Guiǔcacu is an ox’s horn, Vxino tçuno. The damaged initial G and caroned u are read with the surviving strokes, not OCR Cui-.
Guiǔfi is bovine hide, Vxino caua. The short i after Gu corrects OCR r; the final fi is the historical Japanese spelling, not a long-s sequence.

runs.text: Guiǔ-in. i, Riǒbǒ dôxin xite tomonǒ co-

lines.note: Guiǔ-in means accompanying one another with shared intent. Riǒbǒ dôxin describes agreement between the parties; the internal hyphen and the final co- are both printed.

runs.text: Irem dous, ou mais em companhia.

lines.note: To completes co-to. The Portuguese explains two or more people going in company, closing the companionship definition.
Guiǔjin, explained by Cumitçucuſu, means drawing out liquid until exhausted. The headword has a caron and no internal space; a- begins agoa below.
Goa completes a-goa, followed by wine as another liquid that can be drained. The final upright S. labels written usage.

A second Guiǔjin is explained by Suitçucuſu, sucking or drawing everything in. The Portuguese reads Soruer tudo, to swallow everything; the upright Bup. marks Buddhist terminology. This corrects the heavily garbled draft in both languages.
Guiǔmen and Gomen are alternative names for an ox’s face or muzzle, Vxino vomote. Foci- begins focinho across the physical break.
Nho completes foci-nho. The animal is boy, ox, not the OCR bay.
Guiǔnicu is cattle flesh, Vxino nicu. The Portuguese explicitly allows meat from an ox or, on the next row, a cow.
Vaca completes the ox-or-cow distinction in the meat definition. The one-word continuation remains separate.
Guiǔtô is a bovine head, Vxino atama. The u mark is a visible caron, correcting the draft’s grave, while the final o has a circumflex.
Vaca completes the alternative of a cow’s head, rather than only an ox’s head. It closes the preceding entry.

Guiùxeirin names a water-lifting implement likened to a noria. The stem reads xeirin, correcting OCR xerrin. The draft’s grave on u is retained because the small slant is not securely two-armed; a damaged caron, as in the lexical reference’s Guiǔxeirin, remains possible.
Tirar agoa specifies the device’s water-lifting function. Agoa retains its historical vowel sequence.
Guiǔxi is a calf, literally a cow’s child, Vxino co. The explanatory i is followed by a visible comma, not the draft’s period.
Guiǔyǒ pairs cattle and sheep, Vxi, fitçuji. Both length marks are preserved, and the Portuguese directly supplies ox and sheep.
Guixa is a socially polished and refined person. Politico here describes cultivated conduct rather than necessarily a political occupation.

runs.text: ¶ Item, Homem teſo, & tenaz no q̃ diz,

lines.note: The second sense is a firm or tenacious person in what he says. The printed abbreviation q̃ remains unexpanded.
Ou aprende adds what the person learns or takes up to the description of tenacity. It closes the second sense of Guixa.

runs.text: Vigor, ou efficacia com que hum homem

lines.note: Guixei denotes the vigor or effectiveness with which a scrupulous person holds to something. The Portuguese sentence continues across the following rows.

runs.text: muito aprimorado aferra, ou tem mão nalgũa

lines.note: The person firmly grasps or maintains a hold on something. Mão and nalgũa retain their observed nasal-mark positions.
Couſa completes the object of that firmness, correcting OCR conſa. Guixeina fito illustrates a person characterized by this quality; the u corrects OCR a.
Primor and efficacia complete the characterization in the preceding example. This short row belongs to Guixei rather than the next deliberative verb.
Guixi, ſuru, ita means deciding through consultation. The printed verb forms are preserved without expanding or regularizing their abbreviated endings.
Guixiguixi is identified only as a named herb in the gloss. The clear initial G and short ui sequence correct OCR Ciuixiguixi; no botanical identification is imposed.
Guiximecaxi is making a rubbing or grinding noise. The physical eſ- continues as trondo on the next line.

runs.text: trondo esfregando algũa couſa, ou ranjendo

lines.note: The noise may be made by rubbing something or grinding the teeth. Ranjendo has the descending j supported by the repeated Ranjendo below, rather than OCR raniendo.

The example Fauo camiauaxete guixi- describes bringing the teeth together and making the noise. The weak i between cam and auaxete is supported by its surviving upright trace and the Japanese construction; guixi- continues below.
Mecaſu completes guixi-mecaſu. The translation says to make a noise by grinding the teeth; the worn estrondo is a single word, not OCR es. rondo.
Com elles identifies the teeth as what makes the noise. This short continuation closes the example.
Guiximeqi is the corresponding noise-producing or creaking event. The Portuguese reads quandoſe, with o rather than OCR e and the printed close attachment retained.

runs.text: esfrega, ou moe algũa couſa dura, ou ſe ranjẽ

lines.note: The noise occurs when a hard object is rubbed or ground, or when the teeth are ground. The nasal abbreviation in ranjẽ is retained.
Os dentes completes the final object, teeth, before the entry closes. The row is not furniture despite its short length.
Guixin is a doubtful heart or mind, Vtagǒ cocoro. The headword begins with G rather than OCR C; the Portuguese directly confirms the doubt sense.

This second Guixin is a faithful, scrupulous retainer, Yoqi xinca, not the preceding doubtful mind. The Portuguese ends apri-, completed by morado; the r is faint but has a small surviving shoulder between p and i.
Morado completes apri-morado, describing the retainer as accomplished or scrupulous. The weak first strokes do not make this a separate word norado.
Guixiqi is ceremony or solemn procedure. The damaged initial is G rather than OCR C, consistent with the local headword sequence and surviving type.

runs.text: ſe faz algum officio, banquete, caſamen-

lines.note: The ceremony may accompany an office, banquet, or marriage. Caſamen- continues the last noun across the next physical break.
To completes caſamen-to, followed by &c. The short row closes the list of ceremonial occasions.

runs.text: Geſto, ou perſonagem que hũ faz.

lines.note: Guixocu describes the expression or persona a person adopts. The abbreviated hũ remains unexpanded in the Portuguese gloss.
The example concerns giving counsel with a parent’s authoritative manner. Voya and the following Japanese sentence remain roman, while Vt, is italic.

The Portuguese describes giving advice while displaying a father’s manner and authority. Mostrando is the verb, not OCR Mostrande; da remains unaccented because no separate accent can be established over the final a.
Conſelho completes the advice-giving phrase. It is the direct continuation of the previous Portuguese line.

Guixxa is an ox-drawn carriage. Vxiro is retained as the apparent printed form: the r-like shoulder resembles the r in curuma, and no secure second minim establishes n. The intended explanation is evidently Vxino curuma, as the Portuguese and the nearby ox entries show; the worn type leaves a residual r/n uncertainty. Bo continues as is without a visible hyphen.
Is completes bo-is, oxen. The example concerns authorization for a carriage or palanquin; cǒmut continues onto te without a printed terminal hyphen.

Te completes cǒmutte. The Portuguese says the person had permission when traveling in a carriage or Norimono; Norimono is a Japanese noun embedded in the explanation and is printed upright. Tinha corrects OCR tinlha.

runs.text: cença pera entrar diante do Rey.

lines.note: Cença completes li-cença, permission to enter before the king. This row closes the example and precedes the new G-before-O section.

GO, alternatively guio and explained by Von, is the honorific element. The initial G visibly spans two lines and is restored from the draft’s malformed zO; particula and hõ correct OCR particuda and bõ. Hõ continues as ra without a visible hyphen.
Ra completes hõ-ra, honor. Govon illustrates a favor or benefit received from an honored person, whose status is completed below.
Nobre completes the first example’s giver. Gomen then illustrates pardon or permission as another use of the honorific element.
Go is the game played with many small stones. The scan supports pedrinhas and a paragraph mark, not OCR pecrinahas and A; the final Go begins the example continued on f243.
The isolated bottom-right uo repeats the start of f243/c1-l001. It is a catchword, not an extra body continuation; the neighboring border is not a printed l.
